The majority read (الجُمُعَةِ) with a damma on the mim. The first Friday prayer that was performed was the Friday prayer of Sa'd ibn Zurara, who led them in two rak'as and admonished them, so they named it the Day of Friday because of their gathering in it. Then Allah revealed the verse of Friday, so it was the first Friday in which people gathered in Islam. As for the first Friday that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) held, when he arrived in Medina he stopped at Quba' with the Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf, and he stayed there on Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday, and he founded their mosque (p-268). Al-Hasan, Qatada, Malik and others said: it is only the prayer that is performed with tranquility (sakina), and the sa'y is by intention, will and action; it is not hurrying in walking, like the sa'y between al-Safa and al-Marwa. It is only in the sense of His statement: ﴿and that man will have nothing except what he strove for﴾ [al-Najm: 39]. So standing, ablution, dressing, and walking are all sa'y. The apparent meaning is that the address of the command to hasten is to the believers in general, and that it is an obligation upon each individual (fard 'ayn). From some Shafi'is it is reported that it is a communal obligation (fard kifaya), and from Malik there is an isolated narration that it is a sunna. Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: It is established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Going to the Friday prayer is obligatory upon every Muslim." The distance from which one must hasten to the Friday prayer is not addressed by the verse, and the jurists differed on it. Ibn 'Amr, Abu Hurayra, Anas and al-Zuhri said: six miles. It is also said: five. Rabi'a said: four miles. This is reported from al-Zuhri and Ibn al-Munkadir. Malik and al-Layth said: three. Abu Hanifa and his companions said: it applies to those within the city (al-misr), whether they hear the call or not, not to those outside the city even if they hear the call. From Ibn 'Umar, Ibn al-Musayyab, al-Zuhri, Ahmad and Ishaq: it applies to whoever hears the call. From Rabi'a: it applies to whoever, when he hears the call and leaves his house walking, reaches the prayer.

Some of the senior Companions and Successors read (فامْضُوا) (famdu, "proceed") instead of (فاسْعَوْا) (fas'aw, "hasten"). This should be taken as an explanation, in that the sa'y here does not mean hastening in walking, so they interpreted it as proceeding (al-mudiyy). It cannot be considered Qur'an, because it contradicts the consensus of the Muslims' text.

Al-Hasan said: it is recommended (mustahabba). The apparent meaning is that whatever is called remembrance suffices as remembrance of Allah, the Exalted. Abu Hanifa said: if he says "All praise is due to Allah," or "Glory be to Allah," and limits himself to it, it is valid. Others said: there must be speech that is called a sermon, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i, Abu Sufyan and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan. The apparent meaning is that trade is forbidden and that it is invalid. Ibn al-'Arabi said: it is annulled, and this is the sound view. Al-Shafi'i said: it is concluded but not annulled, and every contract that distracts is entirely unlawful in the Law, annulled in piety. End of quotation.

The "bounty of Allah" is what one gains in a good state, such as visiting the sick, maintaining ties with a friend, following a funeral, engaging in buying and selling, and religious and worldly dealings. Along with that, one is commanded to increase the remembrance of Allah. Makhul, al-Hasan and Ibn al-Musayyab said: the bounty commanded to be sought is knowledge. Ja'far al-Sadiq said: it should be the dawn of Saturday morning, meaning that the rest of Friday should be in worship.

It is related that the people of Medina had been afflicted with hunger and high prices, so Dihya arrived with a camel carrying provisions. Mujahid said: it was among their custom that drums and musical instruments entered from its gates, so it entered with them, and they dispersed to see and hear it, and left him (ﷺ) standing on the pulpit with twelve men. Jabir said: I am one of them. Abu Bakr Ghalib ibn 'Atiyya said: they are the ten promised Paradise, and the eleventh is said to be 'Ammar, and it is said Ibn Mas'ud, and it is said eight. They said: then the verse was revealed: ﴿And when they see a trade﴾.

Ibn Abi 'Abla read (إلَيْهِ) with the pronoun referring to amusement (lahw), and both are permissible, as stated by al-Akhfash from the Arabs. Ibn 'Atiyya said: He said "to it" (إلَيْها) and did not say "to both of them," giving precedence to what is more important, since trade was the cause of the amusement, not the amusement the cause of it. Consider how "trade" was placed before "amusement" in the seeing, because it is more important, and it was put last along with the preference so that the mind would first fall upon the more evident. End of quotation.

This should be taken as an explanation, in that the sa'y here does not mean hastening in walking, so they interpreted it as proceeding (al-mudiyy). It cannot be considered Qur'an, because it contradicts the consensus of the Muslims' text.

It is only in the sense of His statement: ﴿and that man will have nothing except what he strove for﴾ [al-Najm: 39]. So standing, ablution, dressing, and walking are all sa'y. The apparent meaning is that the address of the command to hasten is to the believers in general, and that it is an obligation upon each individual (fard 'ayn). From some Shafi'is it is reported that it is a communal obligation (fard kifaya), and from Malik there is an isolated narration that it is a sunna. Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi said: It is established from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Going to the Friday prayer is obligatory upon every Muslim." And they said: the one commanded to hasten is the believer, healthy, free, male, and resident. If others attend, it suffices for them. End of quotation.

The distance from which one must hasten to the Friday prayer is not addressed by the verse, and the jurists differed on it. Ibn 'Amr, Abu Hurayra, Anas and al-Zuhri said: six miles. It is also said: five. Rabi'a said: four miles. This is reported from al-Zuhri and Ibn al-Munkadir. Malik and al-Layth said: three. Abu Hanifa and his companions said: it applies to those within the city (al-misr), whether they hear the call or not, not to those outside the city even if they hear the call. From Ibn 'Umar, Ibn al-Musayyab, al-Zuhri, Ahmad and Ishaq: it applies to whoever hears the call. From Rabi'a: it applies to whoever, when he hears the call and leaves his house walking, reaches the prayer.

Some of the senior Companions and Successors read (فامْضُوا) (famdu, "proceed") instead of (فاسْعَوْا) (fas'aw, "hasten"). This should be taken as an explanation, in that the sa'y here does not mean hastening in walking, so they interpreted it as proceeding (al-mudiyy). It cannot be considered Qur'an, because it contradicts the consensus of the Muslims' text.

The remembrance of Allah here is the sermon (khutba), said Ibn al-Musayyab, and it is a condition for the validity of the Friday prayer according to the majority. Al-Hasan said: it is recommended (mustahabba). The apparent meaning is that whatever is called remembrance suffices as remembrance of Allah, the Exalted. Abu Hanifa said: if he says "All praise is due to Allah," or "Glory be to Allah," and limits himself to it, it is valid. Others said: there must be speech that is called a sermon, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i, Abu Sufyan and Muhammad ibn al-Hasan. The apparent meaning is that trade is forbidden and that it is invalid. Ibn al-'Arabi said: it is annulled, and this is the sound view. Al-Shafi'i said: it is concluded but not annulled, and every contract that distracts is entirely unlawful in the Law, annulled in piety. End of quotation.

The reason trade was singled out among the other prohibited things is that it is what market people most occupy themselves with, since many who come to the cities from the villages gather for commerce when the day rises. So they were commanded to hasten to the trade of the Hereafter and forbidden the trade of this world. The time of prohibition is from the decline of the sun (zawal) until finishing the prayer, said al-Dahhak, al-Hasan and 'Ata'. Others said: from the time of the sermon's call until its completion.

The reference in (ذَلِكم) is to the hastening and leaving trade. The command to disperse and to seek is a command of permission. The "bounty of Allah" is what one gains in a good state, such as visiting the sick, maintaining ties with a friend, following a funeral, engaging in buying and selling, and religious and worldly dealings. Along with that, one is commanded to increase the remembrance of Allah. Makhul, al-Hasan and Ibn al-Musayyab said: the bounty commanded to be sought is knowledge. Ja'far al-Sadiq said: it should be the dawn of Saturday morning, meaning that the rest of Friday should be in worship.

It is related that the people of Medina had been afflicted with hunger and high prices, so Dihya arrived with a camel carrying provisions. Mujahid said: it was among their custom that drums and musical instruments entered from its gates, so it entered with them, and they dispersed to see and hear it, and left him (ﷺ) standing on the pulpit with twelve men. Jabir said: I am one of them. Abu Bakr Ghalib ibn 'Atiyya said: they are the ten promised Paradise, and the eleventh is said to be 'Ammar, and it is said Ibn Mas'ud, and it is said eight. They said: then the verse was revealed: ﴿And when they see a trade﴾.

The majority read (إلَيْها) with the pronoun referring to trade. Ibn Abi 'Abla read (إلَيْهِ) with the pronoun referring to amusement (lahw), and both are permissible, as stated by al-Akhfash from the Arabs. Ibn 'Atiyya said: He said "to it" (إلَيْها) and did not say "to both of them," giving precedence to what is more important, since trade was the cause of the amusement, not the amusement the cause of it. Consider how "trade" was placed before "amusement" in the seeing, because it is more important, and it was put last along with the preference so that the mind would first fall upon the more evident. End of quotation.

In His statement "standing" (قائِمًا) is an indication of the legitimacy of standing during the sermon. The first to sit during the sermon was 'Uthman, and the first to deliver a sermon while seated was Mu'awiya. It was also read (إلَيْهِما) in the dual, referring to the pronoun, like His statement: ﴿If he be rich or poor, Allah is more entitled to both of them﴾ [al-Nisa': 135]. Its explanation is that (أو) is used figuratively and means (و). A different explanation of this was given before, in His statement ﴿Allah is more entitled to both of them﴾ [al-Nisa': 135], in its place in Surat al-Nisa'.

Ending it with His statement ﴿And Allah is the best of providers﴾ was suitable, because they had been touched by some of the high prices, as was mentioned in the occasion of revelation. The commentators have filled much of their pages with rulings and disputes on issues of Friday that have no connection with the wording of the Qur'an.
